problems.stem: A draft screen uses light gray text (#999999) on a white background for body copy. Against WCAG 2.2 AA, which is the correct judgment?
options: It passes, because gray on white is a common, clean look.
It fails AA: body text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, and #999 on white is about 2.8:1, so the text must be darkened.
It passes, because contrast rules apply only to images.
Contrast cannot be evaluated until the final colors are chosen.
problems.explanation: WCAG 2.2 AA (unchanged from 2.1 on this criterion) requires 4.5:1 contrast for normal-size body text. #999 on white falls well short, so this is a measurable failure, not a style preference.

problems.stem: An image of a workflow diagram carries alt text reading "image." Why does this fail an accessibility check even though alt text is present?
options: Alt text must always be at least one sentence long.
Alt text must convey the information the image carries; "image" tells a screen-reader user nothing about the workflow, so the content is still inaccessible.
Decorative images are not allowed to have alt text.
The check fails only if the alt text is missing entirely.
problems.explanation: Present-but-useless alt text is a common failure. Alt text must describe the informational content for users who cannot see the image, not merely exist.

problems.stem: You ask an AI tool to generate alt text for all 12 images in your prototype. It returns fluent descriptions. What is the strongest bounded use?
options: Paste all 12 in, since the descriptions read well.
Check each against what the image must communicate in context, since AI alt text often describes appearance but misses the instructional point the image serves.
Ask the AI to also decide which images are decorative and skip those.
Trust the AI for charts but write your own for photos.
problems.explanation: AI alt text describes what it sees, not why the image is on the page. The designer must confirm each description conveys the image's role in the lesson.

problems.stem: Your draft signals correct answers using a green checkmark and incorrect ones using a red X, with no other difference. Which WCAG concern does this raise, and what is the defensible fix?
options: No concern; red and green are standard for right and wrong.
It relies on color alone to convey meaning, which fails users with color vision deficiency; add a text or shape label so the status is not carried by color alone.
The concern is only that green and red clash visually.
The fix is to make the checkmark and X larger.
problems.explanation: WCAG requires that color not be the only means of conveying information. Pairing the color with text or a distinct shape makes the status perceivable without color discrimination.
